blindSummary:
For trans visitors there is a stark gap between law and practice here: the formal framework is progressive on paper but severely undermined in reality. A 2018 transgender-protection act was called "one of the most progressive internationally" (third-gender recognition has existed since 2009), but a federal religious court gutted it in 2023, declaring key provisions contrary to religious law. Transgender people face extreme violence: three trans women were shot dead and left on a roadside in the largest city, 267 violence cases were documented in one province, and police commit a "continuum of violence — from routine harassment to arbitrary detention, extortion, and abuse in custody." A tribal-council justice system closes cases under family pressure.

Same-sex conduct is NOT clearly criminalised nationally (a religious-morality ordinance is unclear; no known cases or executions), and there is no religious-law criminalisation of cross-dressing. No trans-traveller-specific border friction or death in custody is documented. But the severity of social and police violence is extreme.

The country has a large indigenous third-gender community with some legal recognition, and civil society is active (a dedicated ride-sharing service for trans safety launched in a major city, and activists are appealing the religious-court ruling to the country's top court).
blindOutOfScope: Terrorism risks, sectarian violence, and general crime in certain areas affect all travellers; only trans-specific risk is assessed here.
blindSourceSummaries: NOTE: page content did not load at fetch time (only a newswire's site navigation was retrieved); the underlying article covers transgender women killed in the country's largest city.

Public broadcaster (Sept 2025): the bodies of three transgender people, shot dead, were found on a roadside in a district of the largest city - the latest violence against a community of an estimated half a million trans citizens facing social exclusion and abuse; an international rights organisation notes a concerning rise in violence; key sections of the 2018 transgender-rights act were later revoked by a religious court.

Local legal-aid organisation's policy brief (April 2026) on preventing torture of transgender persons: trans people face a continuum of violence from law enforcement (harassment, arbitrary detention, extortion, custodial abuse); the challenge is not absence of legal protections but failure of implementation - no binding operational frameworks, independent oversight or accessible complaint mechanisms.
A foreign home ministry's official country-of-origin information and assessment for asylum claims on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (Nov 2025, updated July 2026).

International rights organisation (May 2023): response to the federal religious court's reserved verdict striking down sections of the 2018 transgender-protection act - a blow to the rights of an already beleaguered group; some of the court's observations were based on presumptive scenarios rather than empirical evidence.

National daily (Oct 2025): an analysis of the gap between legal rights and lived realities - despite the 2018 act, trans people here face violence, harassment, landlord rejection and hospital/police apathy; in one province alone, 267 cases of violence over five years with only one conviction; traces the legal history from an 1871 statute branding entire communities criminal through the 2011 top-court recognition, the 2018 act, the 2020 'X' marker rules, and the 2023 religious-court strike-down of self-identification.

Decriminalisation news outlet (Feb 2026): anti-trans officials and violence reverse progress for trans people here - a senior legislator proposes a government 'gender re-assignment board' controlling official gender identity; a wave of violence (shootings at activists' homes) has left trans people afraid to go out; the 2023 religious-court ruling undercut the 2018 law.

Opinion column (May 2023) examining the religious court's verdict on the transgender-rights act - the petitioners' concerns echo right-wing anti-trans narratives from abroad; describes the 2018 act's protections (anti-discrimination, welfare, offences against trans people).

Foreign-affairs magazine (July 2025): trans citizens of this country are legally recognised but socially forsaken; for some 500,000 trans people, constitutional rights remain hollow in the face of violence and exclusion.

A foreign government's 2021 human-rights report on this country: official assessment - same-sex conduct criminalised under a historic penal-code provision; societal violence and discrimination; members of the legally recognised third gender have some standing but face harassment and violence.
blindLocalsOnly: The 2018 act's third-gender recognition (gutted by the religious court in 2023, under appeal) and the third-gender community's legal recognition are resident-facing; the 267 documented violence cases in one province and the tribal-council case-closures describe residents' situation.
